newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania parliament in uproar on revolution date.
newsitem.headline: Romania parliament in uproar on revolution date.

text.p: Romania's parliament erupted into uproar on Friday when a session devoted to the seventh anniversary of the revolution that toppled communism broke down into a row over what actually occurred in December 1989.

President Emil Constantinescu, who ousted ex-communist Ion Iliescu in last month's election, said the revolution that overthrew dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was a tragedy and nothing to celebrate. He said Romania's new leaders had a year to establish the truth about its recent history.

Ion Iliescu, who took over as president after Ceausescu's execution and held power for seven years, said the revolution had been carried out by the will of the masses. Dozens of liberal deputies walked out of the hall in protest.

"This is not an anniversary. It is the commemoration of a tragedy, of a sacrifice thanks to which we are here today," Constantinescu told parliament gathered in the opulent palace erected by Ceausescu near the end of his 18-year rule.
"The dead expect from us first of all the truth...If we cannot establish the truth in the year to come we will be unworthy of meeting here in this hall on December 21, 1997."

Liberals say the revolution, in which more than 1,000 people died, was a coup allowing communists to rid themselves of the megalomaniac Ceausescu and retain power. They see the victory by Constantinescu and his centrist backers in elections as the fulfilment of the ideals of the 1989 revolt.
Iliescu, elected last month as a senator, addressed session participants as "comrades in arms" and said the revolution made possible the democratic changes of his seven years in office.

"The communist system was overthrown by the force of the masses and not by an undercover plot or coup d'etat," he said to jeering from some parliamentarians and members of "revolutionary associations" in the public gallery.
"The democratic changes of the past seven years are incontestable. You cannot merely cast aside seven years of basic transformation in Romania's history."

Iliescu was rebuked by Senate chairman Petre Roman, his first post-1989 prime minister, for neglecting to address Constantinescu. Iliescu resumed his speech and addressed the new president, but without referring to him by name.

A few blocks away, several hundred people gathered in University Square to mark clashes with troops and police which culminated in Ceausescu's flight from Bucharest on December 22, 1989 and his execution on Christmas Day.
More commemorations were planned over the weekend.

Seven years after the upheaval, debate rages how the events unfolded and why so many people died. Only about 300 were killed prior to Ceausescu's departure by helicopter from the roof of the Communist Party Central Committee headquarters.
There has never been a clear explanation for why the rest died. Liberals allege that Communists sowed confusion with rumours of terrorist attacks in Bucharest and other cities.
Although dozens of top Communists were jailed for their role in suppressing the revolt, all have since been set free.
In the western city of Timisoara, church bells pealed to mark seven years to the day that the city was proclaimed the first in Romania to be free of communism.
Constantinescu this week attended anniversary ceremonies in Timisoara, where a mass protest on December 16 over the detention of a priest started the revolution.
